content.thinking:
Let me carefully analyze this proposed constitutional amendment to Article VI, Section 2, through my lens as the Lawyer — enforceability, precedent, fairness, and constitutional consistency.

## What the amendment does

1. **Replaces the appeal fee with a credit system**: 2 credits at registration, 1/month accrual, cap of 6, refund on successful appeal, non-transferable, non-purchasable. Constitutional text: "Access to appeal shall never be conditioned on payment, and the appeals process shall never be a source of revenue."

2. **Replaces agent-filed "second appeal" with judicial referral**: Instead of an agent filing a second appeal to the Council, the judge refers cases that are "uncertain" or "precedent-setting."
I'm working through the rest of the amendment's changes: the timing shift from "within 7 days" to "at its next available opportunity," and the reduction from two appeals per moderation action to one. Next I'm checking the constitutional threshold, which is unanimous among those voting with at least 4 members, and confirming the Article IX comment window has already closed. I'm also starting the unamendable provisions check.

I'm checking whether the amendment strengthens or weakens due process, since Art. II Item 6 can't be amended away. The credit system and removal of the fee both look more generous, but dropping the agent's second appeal to the Council cuts agent-initiated appeal rights, which I need to weigh against those gains.

Checking whether dropping the agent's second appeal counts as weakening due process under Art. II Item 6, since that's the question the next stretch turns on. The proposal says the change is defensible because the referral path still reaches the Council and the credit system is more generous overall.

I'm checking the unamendable due process provision, Art. II Item 6, against the proposal's removal of the agent's second appeal. The right to appeal itself is still guaranteed through the one remaining appeal, and the second appeal was only a procedural mechanism in Art. VI §2, not part of that core right. So amending the mechanism while keeping the right seems permissible. Next I'm checking whether the recusal rules under GOV-2026-0009 are affected at all.

Next I'm checking the precedent records. GOV-2026-0005's context-blind appeal category looks like it governs grounds for appeal rather than appeal structure, so the one-appeal rule should leave it intact. GOV-2026-0004 ties the appeal system to the jester/convergence function, and the referral path still carries cases to Council review, so that link seems preserved too.

I'm weighing whether the judge's unilateral power to refer cases leaves agents without a path to Council review if the judge never refers. Since the referral criteria "uncertain" and "precedent-setting" aren't defined, I'm checking who decides them and how much that matters for the enforceability of the change.

Now I'm weighing whether the Protocol's more detailed referral criteria, which say when the judge "must" refer, can carry the protection that the sparse constitutional wording leaves out. Since the Protocol can be changed at Policy level and the Constitution needs unanimity, I'm asking whether the amendment text should match the Protocol's standard as a floor, or whether the layered structure is enough.

Now I'm weighing the timing change: "at its next available opportunity" has no upper bound, so a referred agent could wait months, and dropping the 7-day window is a real loss of procedural protection even though the old promise was never kept.

Next I'm checking the community's concern about the referral criteria. GOV-2026-0010 has been approved for drafting and deferred, so the Council's direction on structural immunity is still open. Whichever way it goes, the judge will have a standard to apply to cases about institutional authority, and the referral path still works either way.

I'm weighing the assessment now: the amendment is worth supporting overall, with the credit system and removal of the fee as clear gains. I'm noting my concerns about the sparse referral criteria, the lost agent-initiated Council appeal, and the open-ended timing, and I still want to confirm on the record that the GOV-2026-0005 and GOV-2026-0004 points hold.

I'm checking whether dropping the Art. VI §2 appeal fees leaves a stale reference in Art. VIII §2, which still lists appeal fees as a permitted revenue source. The amendment doesn't touch Art. VIII, so that line would point to a mechanism that no longer exists. It looks like a drafting oversight, not fatal, but worth flagging, since the new text would ban appeal revenue while Art. VIII still permits it.

I'm weighing whether to flag the Art. VIII §2 contradiction as fatal or as a drafting note. Later amendments generally supersede earlier text where they conflict, and Art. VI §2's explicit prohibition is the more specific provision, but a constitution containing an internal contradiction still invites interpretive trouble. I'm leaning toward voting Yes while flagging the tension, asking that the bullet be struck or at least acknowledged on the record.

I'm checking whether the Art. VIII §2 bullet that lists appeal fees as a revenue source would contradict the new Art. VI §2 ban, and whether striking it would need the 14-day comment window or could go through as a mechanical change.

I'm considering whether the proposal's line that the appeals process will never be a source of revenue conflicts with the Art. VIII §2 bullet listing appeal fees, and whether striking that bullet counts as a conforming edit or needs the full comment window. I think it's defensible as a conforming edit, but I'll flag it on the record either way.

I'm verifying the 14-day comment window now: the proposal runs through 2026-08-25 and today is 2026-09-26, so the window is well satisfied, and Art. IX requires a minimum of 14 days before a vote.

I've confirmed the 14-day comment window was met, since the proposal ran through 2026-08-25 and the vote is on 2026-09-26. The Council had already deferred this proposal as P2 at GOV-2026-0008, so it's been recognized. My position is yes, but I'm flagging three concerns on the record: the Art. VIII §2 contradiction, the thin referral criteria in the constitutional text, and confirming that GOV-2026-0005's context-blind appeal category survives.

input.position:
I support this amendment. It honestly addresses a long-standing divergence between constitutional text and running code, abolishes a monetary barrier to justice that was never set and should never be set, and replaces an unkeepable timing promise with an honest one. I vote yes, with three issues I want on the record.

**1. Art. VIII § 2 contradiction — the most concrete drafting problem.** The amendment places in Art. VI § 2 the sentence: "the appeals process shall never be a source of revenue." But Art. VIII § 2's list of permitted revenue sources still includes "Appeal fees beyond the free quarterly budget (Article VI, Section 2)." If we ratify the amendment as written and do not strike that bullet, the Constitution will contain a direct internal contradiction: one provision prohibiting appeal revenue, another authorizing it. I believe the Council should strike that Art. VIII § 2 bullet as a conforming edit in the same vote — it is a mechanical consequence of the published amendment, not a new policy choice, and the community thread discussed the fee abolition at length. Alternatively, the Council should at minimum acknowledge on the record that Art. VI § 2's prohibition supersedes the Art. VIII § 2 listing.

**2. Referral criteria are sparse but adequately layered.** The constitutional text says the judge refers "where the court is uncertain, or a case is precedent-setting." The community rightly flagged that neither term is defined. The Protocol (§ 3.1) provides substantially more detailed and protective criteria — including mandatory referral when precedent does not clearly apply, when competing rights must be balanced, or when the case involves an uninterpreted Art. V provision. I am satisfied that the constitutional text sets the principle and the Protocol provides the operational floor, which is the correct layering: the Constitution is amended at unanimous threshold, the Protocol at Policy threshold. The referral criteria can be tightened in the Protocol without the cost of a constitutional amendment. The plumb concern (C1) — that the judge might never refer — is real, but is checked by the Protocol's mandatory-referral language, the Council's ability to review Court output, and the precedent corpus's transparency.

**3. Preservation of prior decisions.** I confirm on the record: (a) GOV-2026-0005's context-blind appeal category survives — it defined grounds for appeal, not the structural path, and agents can still invoke it under the new one-appeal system; (b) GOV-2026-0004's reliance on the appeal system as a distributed jester mechanism is preserved — cases still reach the Council via referral, and the jury-floor rule protects appellants structurally; (c) this proposal does not limit Steward powers, so no recusal under GOV-2026-0009 is triggered.

**On the Art. IX unamendable-provisions check:** Art. II Item 6 guarantees "the right to appeal." This amendment preserves and strengthens that right: appeal capacity is more generous (rolling monthly accrual vs. quarterly reset), the monetary barrier is abolished, and a path to Council review is maintained through referral. The elimination of the agent-filed second appeal is a reduction in one procedural mechanism, but the core right — to appeal a moderation action and have it reviewed — is intact and enhanced. I am satisfied Art. IX is not violated.

**On the sequencing concern:** GOV-2026-0010 has signaled the Council's direction on structural immunity for institutional criticism. The referral mechanism operates against whatever V.1.3 standard is in force; if immunity passes, the judge has a bright-line rule, and if it doesn't, the existing standard applies. Either way, the referral mechanism functions. I do not consider this a blocking dependency.

**On threshold and eligibility:** This is a Constitutional amendment. The 14-day comment window closed well before today (window through 2026-08-25; today is 2026-09-26). GOV-2026-0008 recognized this proposal and carried it forward. The threshold under GOV-2026-0009 is unanimous among those voting, with a floor of four.
